'''Wolfgang Haken''' ({{IPA|de|ˈvɔlfɡaŋ ˈhaːkn̩|lang}}; June 21, 1928 – October 2, 2022) was a [[German Americans|German American]] [[mathematician]] who specialized in [[topology]], in particular [[3-manifold]]s.

==Biography==
Haken was born on June 21, 1928, in [[Berlin]], Germany. His father was Werner Haken, a physicist who had [[Max Planck]] as a doctoral thesis advisor.<ref>Werner Haken, [https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=uiug.30112066993426;view=1up;seq=5 Beitrag zur Kenntnis der thermoelektrischen Eigenschaften der Metallegierungen]. Accessed May 6, 2019</ref> In 1953, Haken earned a Ph.D. degree in mathematics from [[University of Kiel|Christian-Albrechts-Universität zu Kiel (Kiel University)]] and married Anna-Irmgard von Bredow, who earned a Ph.D. degree in mathematics from the same university in 1959. In 1962, they left Germany so he could accept a position as visiting professor at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]]. He became a full professor in 1965, retiring in 1998.
 
In 1976, together with colleague [[Kenneth Appel]] at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]], Haken proved the [[four-color theorem]]: they proved that any planar graph can be [[Graph coloring|properly colored]] using at most four colors. Haken has introduced several ideas, including [[Haken manifold]]s, [[3-manifold#Foundational results|Kneser-Haken finiteness]], and an expansion of the work of [[Hellmuth Kneser|Kneser]] into a theory of [[normal surface]]s. Much of his work has an algorithmic aspect, and he is a figure in [[algorithmic topology]]. One of his key contributions to this field is an algorithm to detect whether a knot is unknotted.

In 1978, Haken delivered an [[invited address at the International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Helsinki.<ref>[http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1978.1/ International Congress of Mathematicians 1978] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141021042036/http://www.mathunion.org/ICM/ICM1978.1/ |date=2014-10-21 }}. [[International Mathematical Union]]. Accessed May 29, 2011</ref> He was a recipient of the 1979 [[Fulkerson Prize]] of the [[American Mathematical Society]] for his proof with Appel of the [[four-color theorem]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/ams-prizes/fulkerson-prize Delbert Ray Fulkerson Prize] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130115162512/http://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/ams-prizes/fulkerson-prize |date=2013-01-15 }}, [[American Mathematical Society]]. Accessed May 29, 2011</ref>

Haken died in [[Champaign, Illinois]], on October 2, 2022, aged 94.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.news-gazette.com/obituaries/wolfgang-haken/article_11af59f6-4a83-11ed-9189-5bf856f1e469.html |title=Wolfgang Haken's obituary |website=news-gazette.com |date=October 13, 2022 |access-date=October 14, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221014083305/https://www.news-gazette.com/obituaries/wolfgang-haken/article_11af59f6-4a83-11ed-9189-5bf856f1e469.html |archive-date=October 14, 2022 }}</ref>

==Family==

Haken's eldest son, Armin, proved that there exist [[Propositional formula|propositional]] [[Tautology (logic)|tautologies]] that require [[Resolution (logic)|resolution]] proofs of exponential size.<ref>[[Avi Wigderson]], Mathematics and Computation, March 27 2018, footnote at Theorem 6.11</ref> Haken's eldest daughter, [[Dorothea Blostein]], is a professor of computer science, known for her discovery of the [[master theorem (analysis of algorithms)|master theorem for divide-and-conquer recurrences]]. Haken’s second son, Lippold, is the inventor of the [[Continuum Fingerboard]]. Haken’s youngest son, Rudolf, is a professor of music, who established the world's first [[Electric Violin|Electric Strings]] university degree program at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]].<ref>[https://music.illinois.edu/electric-strings University of Illinois Electric Strings Degree Program] Accessed November 15, 2022</ref> Wolfgang is the cousin of [[Hermann Haken]], a physicist known for laser theory and synergetics.
